fin-01.title: Time Value of Money and Interest
explain: Finance is the study of when and how much money is received and spent. Its starting point is that **100 won today and 100 won one year from now are not the same**, because money received today can be deposited to earn **interest**. This is called the **time value of money**.
The money first deposited is the **principal**, and the percentage charged on the principal is the **interest rate**. There are two ways to calculate interest.

- **Simple interest**: interest is always charged only on the original principal. With principal $P$, interest rate $r$, and $n$ years, $FV = P(1 + rn)$.
- **Compound interest**: interest is also charged on interest that has already been added. $FV = P(1 + r)^n$.
Here $FV$ is the **future value**, that is, the sum of the principal and interest received $n$ years later. Enter interest rates as decimals, for example $10\% = 0.1$.

explain.alt: Bar chart of 100 principal at 10% per year from year 0 to year 3: simple interest (gray) and compound interest (green). Simple interest gives 100, 110, 120, 130, and compound interest gives 100, 110, 121, 133.1.

explain: In the figure, simple and compound interest are equal at year 0 and year 1, because in the first year interest comes only from the principal. From the second year on, compound interest also earns interest on the first year's interest, so the gap keeps widening. All companies and amounts in this book are fictional and exist only for explanation.

fin-02.title: Present Value and Discounting
explain: Lesson 1 asked what money today will become in the future. We can also ask the reverse: **what is money received in the future worth today?** This is the **present value** ($PV$). Converting a future value back to the present using an interest rate is called **discounting**, and the interest rate used is the **discount rate**.
$$PV = \frac{FV}{(1+r)^n}$$

Here $r$ is the discount rate and $n$ is the number of years until payment. The same amount is worth less today the farther away it is in time, and the higher the discount rate, the smaller its present value.

explain.alt: On a horizontal time axis, boxes show 1000 won now, 1100 won after 1 year, and 1210 won after 2 years. An upper arrow says moving right multiplies by 1.1, and a lower arrow says moving left divides by 1.1.

explain: The upper arrow in the figure is the compound interest calculation from Lesson 1 (multiply by 1.1), and the lower arrow is the reverse (divide by 1.1). At a 10% discount rate, 1000 won now and 1210 won two years from now have **equal value**.
Converting to present values lets us compare and add money received at different times on the same basis. This is the foundation for the company valuation and investment decisions in later lessons.

fin-03.title: Risk, Return, and Diversification
explain: In finance, **return** is the gain from an investment as a ratio of the amount invested. If 100 won grows to 110 won, the return is 10%. Future returns are not fixed. Finance calls this uncertainty **risk**.

Here risk means not just the possibility of losing money but **how far outcomes can deviate from expectations**. An asset whose return swings sharply from year to year is risky, and one whose return is nearly constant is low-risk. Higher risk does not guarantee a higher return.
Spreading money across several assets is called **diversification**. When assets rise and fall at different times, the weakness of one is offset by others, so the overall fluctuation shrinks.

explain.alt: Bar chart of annual returns over 4 years. Company A returns 20, -10, 20, -10, and company B returns -10, 20, -10, 20. A 50-50 mix of the two returns 5 every year.

explain: The figure shows two hypothetical companies, A and B. In years when A rises, B falls, and the reverse also happens. Each swings sharply from year to year, but a 50-50 mix gives the same return every year. The return of a mix is the average of the component returns. For example, in year 1 it is $(20 + (-10)) \div 2 = 5$.
Real assets rarely move in exact opposition like this. The figure is deliberately simplified to show the principle and is not a recommendation for any particular investment.

fin-04.title: Raising Funds: Stocks and Bonds
explain: A company needs money to run its business. Raising this money is called **fundraising**, and there are two main routes.

- **Stock**: a slice of the company. A person who buys stock is a **shareholder** and becomes one of the owners of the company. If the company makes a profit, shareholders may receive part of it as a **dividend**, but they have no right to a fixed amount.
- **Bond**: a certificate issued when a company **borrows** money. The person who lends the money is the **bondholder**, a creditor, and has the right to receive the **principal** on a set date along with the agreed **interest**.

A shareholder's return rises or falls with the company's success and is uncertain. A creditor's return is promised, so it fluctuates relatively little. The risk from Lesson 3 appears differently in these two routes.

If a company closes and its remaining assets are distributed, creditors generally are paid first and shareholders afterward. The specific rules differ by country and contract, so this lesson covers only the principle. All companies in this lesson are fictional.

fin-05.title: Firm Value and Financial Statements
explain: A **balance sheet** organizes a company's financial position into a table. The left side lists **assets**, which are what the company owns. The right side shows where that money came from: **liabilities**, which must be repaid to others, and **equity**, which is the portion contributed by shareholders.
$$자산 = 부채 + 자본$$

explain.alt: Balance sheet of a hypothetical company, Saeksal Electronics. Assets of 500 on the left are equal to liabilities of 300 plus equity of 200 on the right, shown with an equals sign.

explain: In the figure, assets of 500 equal liabilities of 300 plus equity of 200. This equation must always hold, because everything a company owns was financed either by borrowing or by money from shareholders. The bonds and stocks from Lesson 4 correspond to liabilities and equity, respectively. A simple measure of how large liabilities are relative to equity is the **debt ratio**.
$$부채비율 = \frac{부채}{자본} \times 100\%$$

Meanwhile, an **income statement** shows the profit over a period, which is revenue minus expenses. If the balance sheet is a snapshot at one point in time, the income statement is a record over a period.

So how do we measure a company's **value**? One method uses the present value from Lesson 2. It converts all the cash the company is expected to generate in the future into present values and adds them up. This value can differ from the asset figures in the books. This lesson is a conceptual introduction and is not a method for valuing real companies or making investment decisions.

fin-06.title: Financial Decisions and Net Present Value
explain: A company must decide whether to spend money on a new project. To compare the costs incurred now with the cash inflows in the future, all of them must be converted to values at the same point in time. This is where the present value from Lesson 2 is used.
**Net present value** ($NPV$) is the sum of the present values of future cash flows minus the initial investment cost.
Here $C_0$ is the cost incurred now, $C_1, C_2$ are the cash inflows one year and two years from now, and $r$ is the discount rate.

A simple textbook criterion is that **a project is acceptable if its NPV is greater than 0 and unacceptable if it is less than 0**. The discount rate reflects the risk of the project. The riskier the project, the higher the discount rate used, and the smaller the NPV. Actual decisions involve many factors beyond this calculation, and this lesson is a conceptual exercise, not investment advice.

fin-07.title: Diversification Effect: How Covariance Reduces Risk
explain: In Stage 1 we saw the intuition of diversification: do not put all your eggs in one basket. This lesson turns that intuition into formulas. The key points are that the risk of a portfolio mixing two assets can be **smaller** than the average of the individual risks, and that the amount of reduction is determined by **covariance**.

If the weights of the two assets are $w_1$ and $w_2$ ($w_1 + w_2 = 1$), the expected return of the portfolio is simply the weighted average: $E[R_p] = w_1E[R_1] + w_2E[R_2]$. Variance does not work this way. $$\sigma_p^2 = w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2w_1w_2\rho_{12}\sigma_1\sigma_2$$ 마지막 항이 두 자산이 함께 움직이는 정도, 공분산이다(통계학의 $\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)$ 공식과 같다). In English: the last term is the covariance, which measures how much the two assets move together; it has the same form as the variance-of-a-sum formula in statistics.

The result depends greatly on the correlation coefficient $\rho$. If $\rho = 1$, then $\sigma_p = w_1\sigma_1 + w_2\sigma_2$, so risk is also a simple weighted average and there is no diversification effect. If $\rho < 1$, $\sigma_p$ is smaller than the weighted average. If $\rho = -1$, a suitable choice of weights can make the risk **exactly 0**. Real stocks usually have $0 < \rho < 1$, so risk can be reduced but not eliminated.

What happens as we increase the number of securities? If we hold $n$ securities in equal weights, the fluctuations unique to each security offset each other and shrink, but the part that moves together with all securities (such as the economy and interest rates) remains. The former is called **unsystematic (idiosyncratic) risk** and the latter **systematic (market) risk**. Diversification can remove only unsystematic risk. This distinction is the starting point of CAPM in Lesson 3.

Limitations: correlation coefficients are estimated from past data and change over time. In particular, during periods such as financial crises, assets that normally have low correlation tend to fall together, and their correlation approaches 1. This means the diversification effect can weaken exactly when it is most needed. This lesson covers concepts and calculations and is not investment advice. All figures are hypothetical.

fin-08.title: The Efficient Frontier and the Sharpe Ratio
explain: In the previous lesson we saw that risk and expected return change with the proportions of two assets. As the number of assets grows, the possible portfolios become countless. Which of them would a rational investor choose? Markowitz answered with a simple principle: **for the same risk, choose the one with the higher expected return, and for the same expected return, choose the one with the lower risk**.

If we plot every possible portfolio with risk (standard deviation) on the horizontal axis and expected return on the vertical axis, the possible portfolios form a region with a curved left boundary. The upper part of that boundary, the set of portfolios with the highest expected return for each level of risk, is the **efficient frontier**. The leftmost point of the boundary is the **minimum-variance portfolio**. Portfolios below the efficient frontier are inefficient choices, because better alternatives exist.

Now add a **risk-free asset** (an asset with zero risk and a certain return $r_f$, such as an idealized short-term government bond). Mixing the risk-free asset with a risky portfolio produces a **straight line** on the risk-return plane. This is because the risk-free asset has zero variance and zero covariance with other assets. The best such line is the steepest one, the line that is **tangent** to the efficient frontier. The point of tangency is the **tangency portfolio**, and this line is called the **capital market line** (CML).

The slope of the line is the excess return per unit of risk, which is the **Sharpe ratio**. $$\text{샤프비율} = \frac{E[R_p] - r_f}{\sigma_p}$$ The higher the Sharpe ratio, the more excess return is earned for the same risk. A striking conclusion is the **separation theorem**. Regardless of risk preference, every investor holds the same tangency portfolio as the risky asset. Investors who want less risk mix in more of the risk-free asset, and investors who want more risk borrow to buy more of the tangency portfolio.

Limitations: the theory assumes that investors consider only expected return and variance, and that the future expected returns, variances, and covariances are known precisely. In practice, expected return estimates are very imprecise, and "optimal" weights computed from past data swing dramatically depending on the sample. Also, if returns are not normally distributed and have fat tails, standard deviation alone cannot capture all of the risk. This lesson is an introduction to theory and not investment advice.

examples.title: Comparing Sharpe ratios
body: Conditions (hypothetical): risk-free return 2%. Portfolio X: expected 8%, standard deviation 12%. Portfolio Y: expected 10%, standard deviation 20%.
Step 1: Sharpe ratio of X $= (8 - 2)/12 = 0.5$, and of Y $= (10 - 2)/20 = 0.4$.

Step 2: Y has the higher expected return, but X offers more reward per unit of risk. Mixing X with the risk-free asset (or borrowing) to match a standard deviation of 20% gives an expected return of $2 + 0.5 \times 20 = 12\%$, which is higher than Y's.

fin-09.title: CAPM and Beta: The Price of Risk
explain: If the conclusion of the previous lesson holds for all investors, then the combination of risky assets held by the whole market becomes the tangency portfolio, that is, the **market portfolio**. Then how are the expected returns of individual assets determined? The **capital asset pricing model** (CAPM) answers this question.

In Lesson 1 we saw that diversification can remove unsystematic risk. The market does not reward risk that can be removed. What investors must bear is only the **systematic risk** that moves together with the market as a whole. The measure of this is **beta**. $$\beta_i = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(R_i, R_m)}{\sigma_m^2}$$ It shows, on average, by what percent the asset moves when the market moves 1%. The beta of the market itself is 1, and the beta of the risk-free asset is 0.

CAPM says that the expected return is directly proportional to beta. $$E[R_i] = r_f + \beta_i(E[R_m] - r_f)$$ 괄호 안 $E[R_m] - r_f$ (the term in parentheses) is the market risk premium. This line is called the **security market line** (SML). The capital market line (CML) has **standard deviation** on its axis and includes only efficient portfolios, while the security market line has **beta** on its axis and includes all assets (in equilibrium).

explain.alt: Horizontal axis is beta β (0 to 2), vertical axis is expected return (% from 0 to 18). A straight line connects the risk-free rate 3% (β = 0) and the market (β = 1, 9%). Point A at (1.5, 14%) lies above the line, and point B at (0.5, 4%) lies below it.

explain: The SML is also used as a valuation tool. If an asset's expected return is **above** the SML, its expected return is high relative to its risk (beta), so it is considered **undervalued**. Buying pressure raises its price, which lowers the expected return back toward the SML. If it is **below** the SML, it is overvalued. CAPM is also widely used to estimate a company's **cost of equity** (the return that shareholders require). It is used again in WACC in Stage 4.

Limitations: CAPM rests on strong assumptions, such as that all investors have the same expectations and can borrow unlimited amounts at the risk-free rate without taxes or transaction costs. Empirical studies have found that beta alone does not sufficiently explain differences in returns, and that other factors such as firm size and value (book-to-market ratio) also play a role (multi-factor models). Even so, the key insight that "only risk that cannot be diversified is rewarded" remains important. This lesson is an introduction to theory and not investment advice.

fin-10.title: Bond Valuation: The Seesaw of Price and Interest Rates
explain: A bond is a bundle of promised cash flows. It pays interest (coupons) on set dates and returns the principal (face value) at maturity. By applying the present value discounting from Stage 1 directly, we can find a bond's price and understand why its price and interest rates move in opposite directions.

The price of a bond with face value $F$, annual coupon $C$, and maturity $n$ years is the sum of all its cash flows discounted at the yield the market requires, $y$ (the **yield to maturity**). $$P = \sum_{t=1}^{n}\frac{C}{(1+y)^t} + \frac{F}{(1+y)^n}$$ The yield to maturity can be interpreted as the average annual return earned if you buy the bond at its current price and hold it to maturity.

explain.alt: Price curve of a bond with face value 100, annual coupon 5, and maturity 3 years. The horizontal axis is market interest rate (yield to maturity, % from 0 to 12) and the vertical axis is bond price (from 70 to 130). The curve slopes downward to the right and is convex downward. Points (3%, 105.7), (5%, 100.0), and (8%, 92.3) are marked.

explain: Three properties shown by the figure: ① **Price and interest rates move in opposite directions.** When rates rise, the present value of the same future cash flows falls, so the price drops. ② If the yield to maturity equals the coupon rate, the price equals face value (**issued at par**). If the market rate is higher than the coupon rate, the price is below face value (**issued at a discount**), and if lower, the price is above face value (**issued at a premium**). ③ The curve is convex, so when rates fall by the same amount, the price rises by more than it falls when rates rise (**convexity**).

Risks of bonds: **interest rate risk** (the price changes as rates change), **credit risk** (the issuer fails to meet its promises), and **reinvestment risk** (interest received is reinvested at a lower rate). The more credit risk an issuer has, the higher the yield investors demand, so its price is lower. The yield difference between government bonds and corporate bonds is called the **credit spread**.

Limitations: this formula assumes that all cash flows are discounted at one single yield. In reality, interest rates differ by maturity (the yield curve), so a more accurate method discounts the cash flow at each point in time using the rate for that maturity. Also, bonds with early redemption features have uncertain future cash flows, so they cannot be valued with a simple formula. This lesson is a conceptual calculation and not investment advice.

fin-11.title: Duration: How Sensitive a Bond Is to Interest Rates
explain: If interest rates rise by 1 percentage point, by what percent does my bond's price fall? In the previous lesson we saw that the longer the maturity and the more cash flows are concentrated later, the more sensitive a bond is to interest rates. **Duration** summarizes this sensitivity in a single number. It is a basic tool banks and insurers use to manage interest rate risk.

**Macaulay duration** is the weighted average of the times when each cash flow is received, where the weight is the share of the bond's price accounted for by the present value of that cash flow. $$D = \sum_{t=1}^{n} t \cdot \frac{PV(CF_t)}{P}$$ It means the average number of years until the cash is returned. The duration of a zero-coupon bond equals its maturity, while a coupon bond pays interest along the way and so has a shorter duration than its maturity.

Price sensitivity is approximated by the **modified duration** $D_{mod} = \frac{D}{1+y}$. $$\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D_{mod} \times \Delta y$$ If the modified duration is 5, a 1 percentage point rise in rates lowers the price by about 5%. The minus sign shows that price and rates move in opposite directions. This approximation is a first-order approximation that uses the **tangent line** to the price curve (a first-order Taylor approximation, as in the math track), so it is accurate for small rate changes.

Factors that increase duration: a longer maturity, a lower coupon rate, and a lower yield to maturity. An **immunization strategy** matches the duration of assets to the duration of liabilities that must be paid in the future, so that the values of assets and liabilities move together when rates change. For example, a company with a pension payment due in 5 years can hold bonds with a 5-year duration to offset the effect of rate changes.

Limitations: duration is a linear approximation, so the error grows when rate changes are large. The actual price curve is convex (bowed downward), so using duration alone overestimates the price drop when rates rise and underestimates the price gain when rates fall. The second-order term that corrects for this is **convexity**. Also, duration assumes that rates of all maturities move by the same amount, but in reality short-term and long-term rates often move differently. This lesson is a conceptual calculation and not investment advice.

fin-12.title: Stock Valuation: The Dividend Discount Model
explain: A bond has promised cash flows, but a stock does not. Dividends are set by the company, and a stock has no maturity. Even so, the basic principle is the same. The intrinsic value of a stock is the **present value of the cash flows that shareholders will receive in the future**. The simplest form is the **dividend discount model** (DDM).

If you hold a stock for one year and sell it, you receive the dividend $D_1$ and the price $P_1$ one year from now. $P_0 = \frac{D_1 + P_1}{1 + r}$. Since $P_1$ is itself determined by the dividends and price after that, continuing this substitution gives $$P_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{D_t}{(1+r)^t}$$ 가 된다. $r$ is the shareholders' **required return** (the cost of equity), which can be estimated with CAPM (Stage 3).

If dividends are assumed to grow forever at a constant rate $g$ each year ($D_t = D_1(1+g)^{t-1}$), the sum of the resulting infinite geometric series gives the **Gordon growth model**. $$P_0 = \frac{D_1}{r - g} \quad (r > g)$$ 식을 거꾸로 쓰면 $r = \frac{D_1}{P_0} + g$, that is, writing the formula backwards, so the required return equals **dividend yield plus growth rate**.

Where does the growth rate $g$ come from? When a company reinvests part of its profit instead of paying it out as dividends, future profits grow. The growth rate can be approximated using $b$, the retention ratio (the share of profit reinvested), and ROE, the return on reinvested equity, as $g = b \times \text{ROE}$. An important insight: reinvestment raises the stock price **only when ROE is higher than the required return $r$**. Reinvesting in a project whose ROE is lower than $r$ produces growth, but it actually reduces value.

Limitations: the Gordon model is extremely sensitive to $g$. With $r = 8\%$, changing $g$ from 3% to 4% reduces the denominator from 5% to 4%, which raises the price by 25%. Also, the formula does not work if $g \ge r$. It cannot be applied directly to growth companies that pay no dividends, so the free cash flow discounting method from Stage 4 is used instead. This lesson is a conceptual calculation and not an actual stock valuation or investment advice. All companies and figures are hypothetical.

Step 2, (C) reinvest 40% with ROE of 5%: $g = 2\%$, $P = 60/0.08 = 750$. The company grows, but its value falls. When ROE < r, reinvestment reduces value.

fin-13.title: Capital Budgeting: NPV and IRR
explain: Companies constantly decide whether to spend money on new factories, new products, and new systems. Decisions like these about long-term investment are called **capital budgeting**. In Stage 1 we saw the basics of net present value (NPV). This lesson compares NPV with the widely used **internal rate of return** (IRR) and covers which one to follow when they conflict.

**NPV** is the sum of all cash flows of an investment discounted at the cost of capital $r$. $NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t}$. If NPV > 0, the investment creates value above the cost of capital, so it is accepted. **IRR** is the discount rate that makes NPV exactly 0. If IRR > cost of capital, the investment is accepted. It is intuitively understood as "the return of this project itself," which is why it is popular in practice.

explain.alt: NPV curve for a project that requires an investment of 1000 and returns 400 each year for 3 years. The horizontal axis is discount rate (% from 0 to 20) and the vertical axis is NPV (from -200 to 200). The curve slopes downward as the discount rate rises, passes through the point (5%, 89), and meets the horizontal axis at point R (about 9.7%).

explain: The **NPV profile** plots NPV against the discount rate. For a typical investment (spending first, receipts later), NPV decreases as the discount rate rises, and the point where the curve meets the horizontal axis is the IRR. In the figure the IRR is about 9.7%. If the cost of capital is 5%, NPV is greater than 0 (about 89), so the project is accepted. If the cost of capital is 12%, NPV is below 0, so the project is rejected. For a single independent project, NPV and IRR lead to the same conclusion.

However, when only one of several **mutually exclusive** projects can be chosen, the two criteria can conflict. This happens when projects differ in scale (a small project can have a high IRR but a smaller total NPV) or when the timing of cash flows differs. In such cases we **follow NPV**, because NPV directly measures the increase in shareholder wealth. Also, if cash flow signs change several times (for example, a large expenditure in the middle), IRR can have multiple values or none at all.

Practical cautions: cash flows are measured as **cash**, not accounting profit, and as **incremental** (the new cash that arises because of the investment). Money already spent (**sunk cost**) is excluded, while the value of resources that could have been used elsewhere (**opportunity cost**) is included. Limitations: NPV depends heavily on the cash flow forecasts and the discount rate, and it does not capture the value of options to expand or abandon a project later (real options). This lesson is a conceptual calculation and not advice on actual investment decisions.

fin-14.title: Revaluing a Firm with Free Cash Flow (FCF)
explain: While the previous lesson measured the value of a single investment, this lesson measures the value of the **whole firm**. A firm is a bundle of many investments. Firm value is the present value of the cash the firm will generate in the future, after making the investments needed to maintain and grow the business, that can be **returned to the providers of capital (creditors and shareholders)**. This cash is called **free cash flow** (FCF).

FCF starts from accounting profit and is adjusted to a cash basis. $$FCF = EBIT(1 - t) + \text{감가상각비} - \text{자본적 지출} - \Delta\text{순운전자본}$$ ① EBIT (operating income) minus taxes is the after-tax profit from operations. ② Depreciation is subtracted as an expense but no cash leaves the firm, so it is added back. ③ Investment in equipment (capital expenditure) takes cash out but is not fully reflected in expenses, so it is subtracted. ④ When inventory or receivables increase, cash is tied up, so the increase in net working capital is subtracted.

Interest is not subtracted from FCF. FCF is cash that belongs to **both** creditors and shareholders, and the effect of the financing method is reflected in the discount rate (WACC, in the next lesson). For this reason, this is called **firm FCF**, and its present value discounted at WACC is the **firm value**. Subtracting net debt from firm value gives the **equity value** of shareholders.

In practice, FCF is estimated individually for the forecast period (usually 5 to 10 years), and beyond that period it is summarized by a **terminal value** assuming steady growth. $$TV_n = \frac{FCF_{n+1}}{WACC - g}$$ This has the same structure as the Gordon model. Firm value = present value of FCF during the forecast period + present value of the terminal value. In many cases the terminal value accounts for more than half of total value.

Limitations: valuation by discounting FCF depends heavily on forecasts. In particular, a small difference between the terminal growth rate $g$ and WACC can change the result dramatically. A commonsense constraint is needed: long-term growth cannot greatly exceed the growth rate of the economy as a whole. For this reason, valuation is reported not as a single number but as a **range** based on assumptions, along with a sensitivity analysis. This lesson is a conceptual calculation and not an actual firm valuation or investment advice.

fin-15.title: Capital Structure: MM Propositions and WACC
explain: A firm can borrow the money it needs (debt) or receive it from shareholders (equity). Does changing the ratio of debt to equity, that is, the **capital structure**, change firm value? In 1958, Modigliani and Miller (MM) gave a striking answer: "In an ideal market, it **does not change**."

**MM Proposition I (no taxes)**: firm value is determined by the cash flows generated by its assets, and it does not depend on how those cash flows are divided between creditors and shareholders. Cutting a pizza into more or fewer slices does not change the size of the pizza. The basis is **arbitrage**. If investors can borrow on their own to replicate the firm's leverage, the firm cannot raise its value by using debt.

**MM Proposition II**: as debt increases, the risk borne by shareholders rises, so the shareholders' required return increases. $$r_E = r_A + \frac{D}{E}(r_A - r_D)$$ $r_A$ is the return on the firm's assets (its business). Debt is cheap, but the more debt is used, the more expensive equity becomes, so the overall cost stays the same. This shows why the intuition that "cheap debt is a gain" is wrong.

In reality there are **taxes**. Interest is recognized as an expense and reduces corporate income tax (the **interest tax shield**). Therefore, when taxes exist, value increases as more debt is used. However, too much debt raises **costs of financial distress** (bankruptcy costs, loss of trading partners, and loss of investment opportunities). The **trade-off theory** holds that the optimal capital structure lies at the point where the tax benefit and the distress costs are in balance.

WACC is used to discount the FCF from the previous lesson and serves as the hurdle rate for new investments with the firm's average risk. The overall cost of capital for the firm is the **weighted average cost of capital** (WACC), where the cost of debt is multiplied by one minus the tax rate to capture the tax shield, V is debt plus equity, and the cost of equity is estimated with CAPM. $$WACC = \frac{E}{V}r_E + \frac{D}{V}r_D(1 - t)$$ $V = D + E$이고, 부채 비용에 $(1 - t)$를 곱하는 것이 세금 절감 효과다. WACC는 앞 교시의 FCF를 할인하는 데 쓰고, 기업의 평균적인 위험을 가진 신규 투자안의 기준 수익률(장애율)이 된다. 자기자본비용 $r_E$는 CAPM으로 추정한다.

Limitations: if all projects are discounted at a single WACC, projects riskier than the firm's average are overvalued and safer projects are undervalued. Projects with different risks should be discounted at rates matching their risks. Also, the principle is to use weights based on **market value**, not book value. This lesson is a conceptual calculation and not advice on actual financing decisions.

fin-16.title: Forwards, Futures, and Hedging
explain: An exporter worries that the won value of dollars it will receive in three months will change with the exchange rate. A flour mill worries that the price of wheat it must buy six months from now will rise. A **derivative** is a contract whose value is determined by the price of another asset (the underlying asset), and it is used to transfer such price risk. The most basic derivatives are forwards and futures.

A **forward contract** is an agreement made now to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specific price (the forward price) on a specific future date. No money changes hands now. At maturity, if the market price is higher than the forward price, the buyer gains, and if it is lower, the seller gains. The buyer's profit at maturity is $S_T - K$, and the seller's is $K - S_T$ ($S_T$ is the market price at maturity and $K$ is the forward price). Because one party's gain is exactly the other party's loss, it is a **zero-sum** contract.

A **futures contract** is a standardized forward that is traded on an exchange. Gains and losses are settled every day as prices change (daily settlement), and participants deposit **margin** for this purpose. The exchange reduces the risk that one party fails to honor the contract (counterparty risk).

**Hedging** means taking a position opposite to an existing risk to offset it. An exporter that will receive 1 million dollars in three months enters a forward contract to **sell** dollars at a set exchange rate in three months. If the exchange rate falls, the won value of the export payment decreases, but the forward contract makes a profit. If the exchange rate rises, the reverse happens. In either case, the won income is **fixed at the forward rate**. Hedging prevents losses but also **gives up the chance of gains**. Its purpose is not profit but the removal of uncertainty.

How is the forward price determined? Buying the asset now and holding it until maturity should give the same result as buying it through a forward contract (no arbitrage). If there are no dividends or storage costs, $K = S_0(1 + r)^T$. Buying now requires borrowing money, so the forward price is higher by the interest on that money. Limitations: if the hedged item and the futures underlying are not exactly the same or do not mature at the same time, the risk is not completely eliminated (**basis risk**). This lesson is conceptual and not advice on actual derivatives trading.

fin-17.title: Options: Payoff Structures of a Right
explain: A forward is an **obligation** to buy. An **option** is a **right** to buy (or sell). Because it is a right, if it is unfavorable you simply do not exercise it. Because of this asymmetry, options are not free: the buyer pays an upfront **premium** (the price of the option). It works somewhat like insurance, limiting losses while keeping the chance of gains.

A **call option** is the right to buy the underlying asset at a set price at maturity (the **strike price** $K$), and a **put option** is the right to sell. The value at maturity is $\max(S_T - K, 0)$ for a call and $\max(K - S_T, 0)$ for a put. The buyer's profit is this value minus the premium. The option seller receives the premium but is obligated to honor the contract if the buyer exercises the right. The profits of the buyer and the seller are exactly opposite.

explain.alt: Two payoff graphs at maturity. (A) Buying a call: profit is constant at -5 when the stock price at maturity is 100 or below, and rises with slope 1 above 100. (B) Buying a put: profit is constant at -4 when the stock price at maturity is 100 or above, and rises with slope 1 as the price falls below 100. The horizontal axis is marked at 80, 100, and 120.

explain: In graph (A), a call buyer with strike 100 and premium 5 does not exercise if the price is 100 or below, so the loss is the premium of 5. Above 100, the profit increases by 1 for every 1 increase in the price. The **break-even point** is $K + \text{프리미엄} = 105$. The loss is limited to a maximum of 5, while the profit is theoretically unlimited. In graph (B), a put buyer with strike 100 and premium 4 profits as the price falls, and the break-even point is $K - \text{프리미엄} = 96$. A put purchase is used like **insurance** against a decline in shares one already owns (a protective put).

Factors that affect option prices: the price of the underlying asset (calls are more expensive when it is higher, puts when it is lower), the strike price, the time to maturity (generally more expensive when longer), **volatility** (higher volatility makes both calls and puts more expensive), and interest rates. The reason volatility raises the value of both options is the asymmetry. The loss on the unfavorable side is limited to the premium, while the gain on the favorable side grows with volatility.

Limitations and cautions: when **selling** an option, the premium received caps the profit, while the loss can be very large (theoretically unlimited for a call sale). Also, the leverage of options produces large percentage gains and losses from small price changes. This lesson covers the principles of payoff structures and is not advice on actual options trading.

fin-18.title: Put-Call Parity and the Binomial Model: The Principle of Option Prices
explain: What is the fair price of an option? The answer given by Black and Scholes (together with Merton) in 1973 transformed financial economics. The core idea is remarkably simple: **if you can build a different portfolio that produces the same result as the option, the price of the option must equal the price of that portfolio** (no arbitrage).

**Put-call parity** holds for a European call and put (exercisable only at maturity) with the same strike price and maturity, as the equation below shows. The left side (a call plus a risk-free bond that pays the strike price at maturity) and the right side (a put plus a share of stock) both give exactly the larger of the stock price and the strike price at maturity, whatever the stock price. If the outcomes are the same, the prices now must also be the same. Therefore, knowing the call price determines the put price. $$C + \frac{K}{(1+r)^T} = P + S_0$$ 가 성립한다. 왼쪽(콜 + 만기에 $K$를 주는 무위험 채권)과 오른쪽(풋 + 주식)은 만기에 어떤 주가에서도 똑같이 $\max(S_T, K)$를 준다.

The **binomial model** shows the principle of option pricing in its simplest form. Suppose that after one period the stock price will be either $S_u$ (up) or $S_d$ (down). By combining $\Delta$ shares of stock with risk-free borrowing, we can build a **replicating portfolio** that produces the same result as the option in both cases. $\Delta = \frac{C_u - C_d}{S_u - S_d}$ is the **delta** of the option, the change in option price for a 1 won change in the stock price.

The same answer can be obtained by using **risk-neutral probabilities** instead of the replicating portfolio. With the risk-free rate $r$, define $q = \frac{(1+r)S_0 - S_d}{S_u - S_d}$. Then $$C_0 = \frac{qC_u + (1-q)C_d}{1 + r}$$ The striking point is that the **probability** that the stock actually rises does not appear in the formula. The option price is determined not by forecasts of the stock price but by the impossibility of arbitrage. If the period is divided into infinitely small steps, the binomial model converges to the **Black-Scholes formula**.

The Black-Scholes model assumes that the stock price moves continuously with a constant volatility (lognormal distribution) and that the replicating portfolio can be adjusted at any time without transaction costs. Of the five inputs (stock price, strike price, maturity, interest rate, and volatility), only **volatility** is not directly observed. Therefore, the **implied volatility**, calculated backward from market option prices, is used as an indicator of market uncertainty. Limitations: actual stock prices have sudden jumps and volatility changes over time, so a "volatility smile" is observed, where implied volatility differs across strike prices. This lesson is an introduction to principles and not trading advice.

fin-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Valuing a Hypothetical Firm and Checking Its Risks
explain: The first lesson of the capstone values one hypothetical company, "Haeoreum Electronics," using the tools of Stages 2 to 5. It connects, in order, estimating the discount rate (CAPM, WACC), estimating cash flows (FCF), calculating value (terminal value), and checking risk (sensitivity and hedging). All figures are hypothetical and this is not an actual company valuation.
**Step 1 (cost of equity)**: Haeoreum Electronics has a beta of 1.2, a risk-free rate of 3%, and a market risk premium of 5%. By CAPM, $r_E = 3 + 1.2 \times 5 = 9\%$.
**Step 2 (WACC)**: market-value weights are 75% equity and 25% debt, the cost of debt is 5%, and the corporate tax rate is 20%. $WACC = 0.75 \times 9 + 0.25 \times 5 \times 0.8 = 6.75 + 1 = 7.75\%$.

**Step 3 (FCF and value)**: if next year's EBIT is 200, depreciation is 30, equipment investment is 40, and the increase in net working capital is 10, then $FCF_1 = 200 \times 0.8 + 30 - 40 - 10 = 140$. Assuming a perpetual growth rate of 2.75%, firm value $= 140/(0.0775 - 0.0275) = 140/0.05 = 2800$. If net debt is 700, the equity value of shareholders is 2100.

**Step 4 (sensitivity)**: if the growth rate is lowered by 1 percentage point ($g = 1.75\%$), value $= 140/0.06 \approx 2333$, and if raised by 1 percentage point, $140/0.04 = 3500$. A change of ±1 percentage point in growth moves value between −17% and +25%. The result should be reported as a **range**, not as a single number.

**Step 5 (risk check)**: 40% of Haeoreum Electronics' revenue comes in dollars. If the exchange rate falls 10%, FCF could decline significantly. Fixing part of next year's dollar income with forward contracts (Stage 5) reduces the variability of FCF, which also reduces the uncertainty of the valuation and the risk of financial distress. However, hedging also gives up the gains when the exchange rate moves in a favorable direction.

fin-20.title: Capstone: Valuation Report and Risk Management Design
explain: The final task is to **set up one hypothetical company, value it, diagnose its major financial risks, design a management plan, and critique your own analysis**. It is not a task of valuing an actual company or security, and it is not advice for investment, lending, or tax decisions.

Report outline: ① **Company setup**: business, revenue structure, and capital structure (hypothetical figures). ② **Discount rate**: cost of equity by CAPM, the WACC calculation, and its basis. ③ **Cash flows and value**: the basis for the FCF estimate, growth assumptions, and firm value and equity value of shareholders. ④ **Sensitivity**: the value range according to WACC and growth (or a key revenue assumption). ⑤ **Risk diagnosis and management**: which of interest rate, exchange rate, commodity, and credit risks matter most, which tools will manage them (forwards, options, capital structure adjustment, and so on), and their costs and what is given up. ⑥ **Critique**: the conditions under which the model's assumptions (CAPM, perpetual growth, stable capital structure) break down.

Principles of good financial analysis: attach a **basis** to every number. Do not stack optimistic assumptions on top of each other. Report results as a **range**. In risk management, state not "eliminate the risk" but "which risk is retained, how much is transferred, and what is the cost of doing so."
